Q22009876.summary: The Mother of God sits on a high throne holding the Christ Child, who blesses, while Saints Anthony and Theodosius, founders of the Kyiv Monastery of the Caves, stand at either side with unfurled scrolls. It is the earliest surviving image of these two founding monks. The Christ Child, held at the centre of the composition, shows that the monks' prayers are offered to the incarnate Lord.
facts: Saint Anthony's scroll carries a monastic exhortation, rendered in the Russian Wikipedia article as 'I pray you, children: let us keep to abstinence and not be idle, for we have the Lord as our helper.'
Tradition holds that in 1288 Prince Roman of Bryansk was healed of blindness before this icon and founded the Svensky Monastery, where it stayed until 1925; it is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.
The panel measures 67 × 42 cm.
Q22009876.notes: Dating is disputed. The Commons description (citing the Tretyakov Gallery) gives c. 1288; some scholars (e.g. Konrad Onasch, per French Wikipedia) and the traditional attribution to Alypius place it in the 11th–12th century. Wikidata records both. Corrected to c. 1288, which moves it out of this batch's centuries.

Q80079053.summary: For the first time in history, Christ's face appeared on a coin when Emperor Justinian II placed his bust on the front of the gold solidus, relegating his own portrait to the reverse. On this coin from his second reign, Christ is shown with short curly hair and a close beard, raising his hand in blessing and holding the Gospels, encircled by the words 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. Carried in purses across the Mediterranean, it made the image of Christ the guarantor of the empire's wealth and power.
facts: Justinian II first put Christ on his coinage around 692, using a long-haired, bearded Pantocrator type; during his second reign (705–711) he introduced this younger, curly-haired type.
On his first-reign coins the emperor, shown on the reverse, calls himself 'servus Christi', the servant of Christ.
The new coinage may have prompted the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik to introduce purely inscribed, imageless Islamic coins in the 690s.

Justinian's successors dropped the image of Christ after his death in 711, and through the period of Iconoclasm it did not return until the reign of Michael III, after the restoration of icons in 843.
Q80079053.notes: Dated 705 by the museum (start of Justinian II's second reign, 705–711).

cur:catacombs-lazarus-peter-fragment-314.summary: At the left of this fragment, the young Christ, holding a scroll, reaches towards the swaddled Lazarus standing in his temple-like tomb, while Martha kneels at his feet; to the right, soldiers lead Peter away under arrest and a cock recalls his denial. The carving is crisp and expressive, the faces individualised.
facts: The museum describes the scenes as the raising of Lazarus, the arrest of Peter, and an orans reworked as the denial of Peter.
The small cockerel at the lower right alludes to Christ's prophecy of Peter's denial.

cur:catacombs-arles-traditio-legis.summary: Five arched niches frame the scenes; at the centre Christ stands on the hill of paradise with its four rivers and hands the unrolled scroll of the Law to Peter, while Paul acclaims him. Other niches show further biblical scenes with the apostles. The Traditio Legis presents Christ as the lawgiver of the new covenant.
facts: Commons records that it comes from the Alyscamps cemetery of Arles and is carved from Carrara marble (FAN.92.00.2487).
A second Commons photograph of the same sarcophagus (Arles sarcophagus with christ.jpg) shows it from a different angle.

cur:objects3-paschal-enamel-cross-silver.summary: This silver box was made to hold the enamelled cross-reliquary of Pope Paschal I. On its lid a bearded, haloed Christ sits enthroned and blesses, holding a book, between St Peter with his cross-staff and St Paul with a codex, while two winged angels look on from roundels above and small figures are worked at the foot of the throne. Gilded against the silver ground, the lid presents Christ as Lord of the Church, guarded by the apostles of Rome.
facts: The case belongs to the enamelled cross of Paschal I (Vatican inv. 61881), one of the treasures kept in the Lateran chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum.
The Sancta Sanctorum acquired the enamelled cross commissioned by Paschal I (pope 817–824) among the relics added over time to the chapel's treasury.

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with museum label)

cur:objects3-paschal-enamel-cross-silver.notes: The Vatican label (quoted on Commons) says only 'perhaps Rome, 9th century'; association with Paschal I's pontificate follows from its function as the case of his cross. The identifications of Christ, Peter and Paul rest on their attributes. The cross itself (cur:objects2-paschal-enamel-cross) and the separate silver cruciform case (cur:objects2-paschal-silver-cruciform-case) are already in the collection; this is a different object.

walters:W.72.98R.summary: At the top of the page Christ sits on a rainbow in a green-bordered mandorla against a blue ground, blessing with his right hand and holding an open book. Crowds of saints stand on either side, among them the Virgin and John the Evangelist, and below a tonsured monk kneels and stretches up a scroll towards Christ's feet. The lively pen drawing, lightly coloured, introduces a text written for the instruction of religious women.
facts: The manuscript was written at the Cistercian abbey of Himmerode in Germany in the early 13th century; an erased 15th-century ownership note names the monks of Himmerode.

The Speculum Virginum ('Mirror of Virgins') is a 12th-century dialogue between a teacher, Peregrinus, and a student, Theodora, on the religious life of women; its authorship is uncertain, with Conrad of Hirsau one proposed author.
The Walters describes its copy as one of twenty-two surviving Latin manuscripts of the text, with twelve illustrations.
walters:W.72.98R.notes: Museum date 1200–1225; the 7th-century date in our data was an import error. The Walters credits Conrad of Hirsau as author of the text, not as artist.

walters:W.432.1R.summary: The Virgin, in a blue mantle against a red ground patterned in gold, reads from an open book while the naked Christ Child on her lap stretches out his hand toward the page. An angel in a golden robe stands at the right, offering a fruit, and more fruit lies on the green ledge in front. Above runs the rubric of the 'Obsecro te', the prayer this miniature introduces at the very start of the book.
facts: This miniature on fol. 1r accompanies the 'Obsecro te', a late medieval prayer to the Virgin.
The book was made in Leiden in the first quarter of the 16th century; its Walters description notes nearly sixty small miniatures.

links.label: The Digital Walters: Prayer Book with Passages from the Gospels (W.432)

walters:W.432.1R.notes: Origin in Leiden and the date 1500–1525 follow the Walters manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters). The worklist year (800) was a parsing error for '1st quarter 16th century'.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.summary: Following the ancient custom of dining, Christ and the twelve apostles recline around a semicircular table. Christ, haloed and robed in purple, lies at the place of honour on the left, while the apostles crowd in a tight arc behind a white cloth set with loaves and a large dish holding two fish. Rather than the moment of the bread and cup, the mosaic shows the company gathered at table, a memorable early image of the Supper on the eve of the Passion.
facts: The Passion scenes on the upper south wall correspond to the Gospel passages read aloud in the church during Lent under Theodoric.
The narrative panels were executed by at least two artists, and the mosaics were renovated and altered in the mid-19th century by Felice Kibel.
